notes: Launch sites for the kid-friendly mission planner. Labels: Fact = official/agency/primary source (agency page, launch-vehicle user's guide, press kit); Reported = secondary source (mainly Wikipedia, which cites primaries); Inference = derived by us (e.g. minimum inclination = site latitude). lat/lon are decimal degrees (N/E positive) of the main orbital pad, rounded to 3 decimals. allowed_inclination_deg = [min, max] orbit inclination for orbital launches as published or as actually flown; inclination_certainty says whether it is 'published' (range-safety/user-guide numbers), 'typical' (built from flown missions, not an official limit) or 'uncertain'. Inclinations above 90 deg are retrograde (the orbit goes 'backwards' against Earth's spin, so the spin bonus becomes a penalty); ~97-99 deg is sun-synchronous. Rockets can reach inclinations below the site latitude only with an expensive 'dog-leg' turn or later plane change (examples noted per site). Earth-spin bonus is not stored: compute 465.1 m/s x cos(latitude) for a due-east launch, or 465.1 x cos(inclination) for the eastward component of a given orbit.

sites.name: Kennedy Space Center / Cape Canaveral Space Force Station
sites.coord_source: SpaceX Falcon User's Guide (May 2025), sec. 8: LC-39A at 28.6082 N, 80.6041 W
sites.inclination_notes: Falcon User's Guide (2025) Eastern Range table: LEO 28.5-55 deg normal; 55-65 deg possible with a performance-costing dog-leg; GTO/GSO up to 28.5 deg; polar/SSO 85-105 deg also flown from the Eastern Range in specific cases (SpaceX discretion) by a southward corridor along the Florida coast. Below 28.5 deg is possible only with a performance penalty. Wikipedia's LC-39A infobox (citing the 2021 guide) lists 28.5-55 and 66-145 deg.
sites.typical_launch_direction: East over the Atlantic Ocean (northeast for the Space Station, southeast toward the equator for geostationary orbits)
famous_launches: Artemis I, 2022 (uncrewed SLS/Orion around the Moon)
Artemis II, 1 April 2026 (first crew around the Moon since 1972)
moon_missions_examples: Artemis I (2022) and Artemis II (2026) from LC-39B
Intuitive Machines IM-1 lander (2024) from LC-39A
sites.fun_fact: All the crewed Moon missions in history - every Apollo landing and Artemis II in 2026 - started their trip from the Florida coast.
sites.why_here: It is about as far south as the mainland United States reaches with open ocean to the east, so rockets get a bigger Earth-spin boost and drop their used stages into the Atlantic instead of on towns.

sites.name: Vandenberg Space Force Base
sites.coord_source: SpaceX Falcon User's Guide (May 2025), sec. 8: SLC-4E at 34.6320 N, 120.6107 W
sites.inclination_label: Fact (min, 2025 guide) / Reported (max 145 deg: Wikipedia SLC-4 infobox citing the 2021 Falcon User's Guide)
sites.inclination_notes: Falcon User's Guide (2025) Western Range table: 55-65 deg (shared with Eastern Range), 65-85 deg, polar/SSO 85-105 deg, retrograde 105+ deg. Launches head south (or south-southwest/southeast) over the Pacific; launching east would fly over California, so low inclinations are not offered.
sites.typical_launch_direction: South over the Pacific Ocean (toward the South Pole for polar orbits)
famous_launches: Discoverer 1, 1959 (world's first satellite in a polar orbit)
DART, 2021 (NASA spacecraft that crashed into an asteroid to nudge it)
moon_missions_examples: Clementine (Titan II from SLC-4W, 25 Jan 1994) - mapped the Moon from lunar orbit
sites.fun_fact: Rockets from Vandenberg fly south, so their satellites end up circling over the North and South Poles and can see every part of Earth as it spins underneath.
sites.why_here: The California coast bends so that south of Vandenberg there is only open Pacific Ocean all the way to Antarctica, which makes it safe to launch into polar orbits.

sites.name: SpaceX Starbase
sites.pad: Starbase orbital launch site (Orbital Launch Pads 1 and 2), Boca Chica
sites.coord_source: Wikipedia 'SpaceX Starbase' launch-site coordinate (25.997, -97.157); pad-level coordinates for OLP-2 not found in an official source
sites.inclination_label: Inference (min = site latitude) / Reported (max: Starship Flight 15 orbit, 30.5 deg)
sites.inclination_notes: No published inclination range found. All Starship flights launch east over the Gulf of Mexico. Early flights were sub-orbital tests; Flight 15 (13 Nov 2026) reached orbit at 30.5 deg inclination (Wikipedia, NASASpaceFlight). The range given is only what geometry and flown missions show, not a range-safety limit.
sites.typical_launch_direction: East over the Gulf of Mexico, passing between Florida and Cuba
famous_launches: Starship Flight 5, Oct 2024 (first Super Heavy booster caught by the tower arms)
Starship Flight 15, 13 Nov 2026 (ship reached orbit, released 26 Starlink satellites, and was caught by the tower on return)
sites.fun_fact: SpaceX catches its giant Starship rockets out of the air with two huge metal arms on the launch tower, nicknamed 'chopsticks'.
sites.why_here: It is at the southern tip of Texas with the Gulf of Mexico to the east, so rockets fly over water and get a good Earth-spin boost from a low latitude.

sites.name: Guiana Space Centre (Centre Spatial Guyanais)
sites.coord_source: Wikipedia 'ELA-4' infobox (5.265 N, 52.792 W). The Ariane 6 User's Manual (Issue 2, 2021) lists pad coordinates only as 'TBC' with a typo, so it is not used.
sites.inclination_label: Fact (6 deg GTO and 'almost all orbit inclinations can be accessed from the CSG': Ariane 6 User's Manual) / Reported (~98 deg upper end = sun-synchronous missions typically flown northward by Vega)
sites.inclination_notes: Ariane 6 standard GTO and lunar-transfer orbits are 6-7 deg; the manual also quotes ISS (51.6 deg) performance and says almost all inclinations are reachable (east over the Atlantic for low inclinations, north for polar/SSO). No published hard min/max azimuth limits found; the max here is typical, not a limit. Note 6 deg is just above the 5.3 deg site latitude.
sites.typical_launch_direction: East over the Atlantic Ocean for geostationary and Moon missions; north over the Atlantic for polar orbits
moon_missions_examples: SMART-1 (Ariane 5 from ELA-3, 27 Sep 2003) - ESA lunar orbiter
sites.fun_fact: The James Webb Space Telescope, the biggest space telescope ever built, blasted off from this jungle spaceport on Christmas Day 2021.
sites.why_here: Kourou is only about 5 degrees north of the equator with open sea to the east and north, so rockets get almost the full 465 m/s Earth-spin boost and can reach low-inclination orbits cheaply.

sites.name: Baikonur Cosmodrome
sites.coord_source: Wikipedia 'Baikonur Cosmodrome' pad table (Site 31/6: 45.996 N, 63.564 E)
sites.inclination_label: Reported (Wikipedia pad infobox, Site 31 and Site 1/5) / Fact for the discrete Soyuz corridors
sites.inclination_notes: Launches may only use approved azimuths because spent stages must fall in designated drop zones in Kazakhstan/Russia. Starsem Soyuz User's Manual (2001), Table 2-1, approved direct-ascent corridors: azimuth 60.7 -> 51.8 deg, 34.8 -> 64.9 deg, 25.9 -> 70.4 deg, -10.9 -> 95.4 deg inclination. The ISS orbit (51.6 deg) was chosen partly so Baikonur could reach it. Site 31/6 was damaged on 27 Nov 2025 (service platform collapse after Soyuz MS-28) and returned to service in 2026 (Wikipedia lists a launch on 16 Sep 2026).
sites.typical_launch_direction: Northeast over the Kazakh steppe (toward the Space Station's 51.6 deg orbit)
famous_launches: Vostok 1, 1961 (Yuri Gagarin, first human in space)
Luna 9, 1966 (first soft landing on the Moon)
moon_missions_examples: Luna 2 (1959, first object to reach the Moon)
Luna 9 (1966, from Site 31/6, first soft landing)
sites.fun_fact: The first satellite (Sputnik 1) and the first person in space (Yuri Gagarin) both launched from Baikonur, and astronauts still fly from here to the Space Station on Soyuz rockets.
sites.why_here: It was built in the flat, empty Kazakh steppe, far from cities and borders, with room downrange for spent rocket stages to fall on land; it is not close to the equator, so it gets less Earth-spin help.

sites.name: Wenchang Space Launch Site
operators: China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC)
sites.coord_source: Wikipedia 'Wenchang Space Launch Site' (LC-101 at 19 deg 36' 52.17" N, 110.951 E)
sites.inclination_label: Inference (min = site latitude) / Reported (max: sun-synchronous missions flown by Long March 8)
sites.inclination_notes: No official azimuth/inclination limits found. Flown missions include geostationary-transfer and Moon/Mars departures (low inclination, east), Tianzhou/Tiangong module flights to ~41.5 deg, and sun-synchronous orbits (e.g. Long March 8, 27 Feb 2022, 22 satellites). Wikipedia's unsourced claim of '90 to 175 degrees' looks like azimuths, not inclinations, and is not used.
sites.typical_launch_direction: East or southeast over the South China Sea / Pacific
famous_launches: Chang'e 6, 3 May 2024 (first samples from the Moon's far side)
moon_missions_examples: Chang'e 7 was rolled out here in Aug 2026 but postponed to 2027 (not yet launched)
sites.fun_fact: China's biggest rocket, the Long March 5, travels to Wenchang by ship from the port of Tianjin instead of by train like rockets for China's inland launch sites.
sites.why_here: Hainan is the part of China closest to the equator (about 19 degrees north), has a seaport for delivering huge rockets, and lets spent stages fall into the sea instead of on villages.

sites.name: Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center
sites.pad: Launch Area 4, SLS-1 (Long March 2F / Shenzhou crewed launches)
sites.coord_source: Wikipedia 'Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center' (SLS-1: 40.957893 N, 100.290944 E)
sites.inclination_label: Inference (min ~ site latitude; Tiangong/Shenzhou orbit ~41.5 deg) / Reported (sun-synchronous ~97-98 deg)
sites.inclination_notes: No published azimuth limits found. Wikipedia: JSLC is used for low- and medium-Earth orbits with high inclination. Typical flown orbits: ~41.5 deg (Shenzhou to the Tiangong station; Shenzhou 5 was ~42.4 deg) up to ~97-98 deg sun-synchronous. Because it is inland, spent stages fall on land, which restricts launch directions; it does not launch to geostationary orbit or the Moon.
sites.typical_launch_direction: Southeast over the desert for the space station (~41.5 deg); south for polar/sun-synchronous orbits
famous_launches: Shenzhou 5, 2003 (Yang Liwei, China's first astronaut in space)
Every Chinese crewed Shenzhou flight to the Tiangong space station
sites.fun_fact: Every Chinese astronaut so far has blasted off from this spaceport in the middle of the Gobi Desert.
sites.why_here: It is in a remote, dry, almost empty desert where the weather is clear most of the year and falling rocket stages land far from people; being far from the equator is a trade-off it accepts.

sites.name: Tanegashima Space Center
sites.pad: Yoshinobu Launch Complex (H3 flies from Launch Pad 2, LA-Y2)
sites.coord_source: Wikipedia 'Yoshinobu Launch Complex' (30 deg 24' 08" N, 130 deg 58' 30" E); complex-level, not pad-level
sites.inclination_notes: MHI H-IIA User's Manual (Ver. 4.0) standard missions: GTO 28.5 deg (slightly below the 30.4 deg latitude via a dog-leg), LEO 30.4 and 51.6 deg, SSO 98.6 deg. These are the published standard orbits, not a stated range-safety min/max. JAXA's H3 press kit (Oct 2026): initial inclination from Tanegashima is ~28.5 deg; a long-coast burn can lower GTO inclination to ~20 deg. H3 test flight 2 flew on azimuth 90.8 deg over the Pacific.
famous_launches: MMX, 20 Oct 2026 (H3 F10, mission to Mars' moon Phobos and back)
sites.famous_launches_label: Fact (MMX: JAXA press release) / Reported (Kaguya, SLIM: Wikipedia launch tables)
sites.fun_fact: Japan's MMX spacecraft, which will try to bring back the first-ever sample from a moon of Mars, launched from this island on 20 October 2026.
sites.why_here: It is an island in the far south of Japan with open Pacific Ocean to the east and south, so rockets can climb over the sea away from Japan's crowded main islands.

sites.name: Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC SHAR)
sites.pad: Second Launch Pad (SLP: LVM3 / GSLV, Chandrayaan-2 and -3)
sites.coord_source: Wikipedia 'Satish Dhawan Space Centre' (SLP: 13.7199 N, 80.2305 E)
sites.inclination_label: Fact (min: PSLV-C55 to 10.00 deg on launch azimuth 104 deg, ISRO brochure) / Reported (max ~98 deg sun-synchronous, typical)
sites.inclination_notes: 10 deg is below the 13.7 deg latitude, so it needs a dog-leg. Polar/sun-synchronous launches go southeast (azimuth ~140 deg or more) and then turn to avoid flying over Sri Lanka (India Today, Reported). No official min/max azimuth table found.
sites.typical_launch_direction: East-southeast over the Bay of Bengal; polar launches go south-southeast with a turn around Sri Lanka
famous_launches: Chandrayaan-1, 2008 (found water molecules on the Moon)
Chandrayaan-3, 2023 (first landing near the Moon's south pole)
sites.fun_fact: Sriharikota is an island between a big lagoon (Pulicat Lake) and the Bay of Bengal, and India's Chandrayaan-3 lander flew from here to become the first to land near the Moon's south pole.
sites.why_here: It sits on India's east coast fairly close to the equator, so rockets launch east over the sea with a good Earth-spin boost and a large empty safety zone.

sites.name: Rocket Lab Launch Complex 1
sites.coord_source: Rocket Lab Electron Payload User Guide 8.0 (Sept 2025): LC-1 at 39.262 S, 177.865 E
sites.inclination_notes: Electron Payload User Guide 8.0: from LC-1, trajectories of 39 to 120 deg inclination; other inclinations possible on request. The Kick Stage can also change planes after launch (CAPSTONE used this to leave for the Moon).
sites.typical_launch_direction: East over the Pacific for mid inclinations, or south toward Antarctica for sun-synchronous orbits
famous_launches: 'Still Testing', 21 Jan 2018 (first Electron to reach orbit)
moon_missions_examples: CAPSTONE (Electron + Lunar Photon, 28 Jun 2022) - first spacecraft to fly the NRHO orbit planned for Artemis
sites.fun_fact: This was the first privately owned spaceport ever to launch a rocket toward orbit, and in 2022 a tiny NASA spacecraft called CAPSTONE left from here for the Moon.
sites.why_here: The tip of the Mahia Peninsula has open ocean to the east and south and very little air or sea traffic, so Rocket Lab can launch often and reach many different orbits.
